[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 75 · 7.3.1 Recommended maintenance program
Abbreviation used in maintenance program:
- V = Visual checking
- C = Cleaning
- D = Disassembling and assembling
- R = Reconditioning or replacement
- T = Testing and measurement.
Not all options are applicable for all machines.

[2] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 74 · 7.3 Maintenance program
This chapter presents a recommended maintenance program for ABB machines. This maintenance program is of a general nature, and should be considered as a minimum level of maintenance. Maintenance should be intensified when local conditions are demanding or very high reliability is required. It should also be noted that even when following this maintenance program, normal supervision and observation of the machine's condition is required.
Please note that even though the maintenance programs below have been customized to match the machine, it might contain references to accessories not available on all machines.
The maintenance program is based on four levels of maintenance, which rotate according to operating hours. The amount of work and down time vary, so that level 1 includes mainly quick visual inspections and level 4 more demanding measurements and replacements. More information about the spare part packages suitable for these maintenances can be found in Chapter 9.2 Spare parts for rotating electrical machines. The recommended maintenance interval can be seen in Table 6 Maintenance intervals. The operation hour recommendation in this chapter is given as equivalent operating hours (Eq. h), that can be counted by the following formula:

[3] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 73 · 7.1 Preventive maintenance
A rotating electrical machine often forms an important part of a larger installation and if it is supervised and maintained properly, it will be reliable in operation and guarantee a normal lifetime.
The purpose of maintenance is therefore to:
- Secure that the machine will function reliably without any unforeseen actions or interventions
- Estimate and plan service actions in order to minimize down time.
The difference between supervision and maintenance is rather diffuse. Normal supervision of operation and maintenance includes logging of operating data such as load, temperatures, vibrations, as well as verification of the lubrication, and measurement of the insulation resistances.
After commissioning or maintenance, the supervision should be intensive. Temperature of bearings and windings, load, current, cooling, lubrication and vibration shall be checked frequently.
This chapter presents recommendations regarding maintenance program, and work instructions how to conduct common maintenance tasks. These instructions and recommendations should be read carefully and be used as a basis when planning the maintenance program. Note that the maintenance recommendations presented in this chapter represent a minimum level of maintenance. By intensifying maintenance and supervision activities, the reliability of the machine and the long-term availability will increase.
The data obtained during supervision and maintenance is useful for estimating and planning additional service. In case some of this data indicates something out of the ordinary, the trouble shooting guides in Chapter 8. Trouble shooting, will aid in locating the reason for the trouble.
ABB recommends the use of experts in the creating maintenance programs, as well as in performing the actual maintenance and possible trouble shooting. The ABB Motors and Generators Service organization is happy to assist in these issues. The ABB After Sales contact information can be found in Chapter 9.1.3 Contact information for Motors and Generators Service.
An essential part of the preventative maintenance is to have a selection of suitable spare parts available. The best way to have access to critical spare parts is to keep them on stock. Ready-made spare part packages can be obtained from the ABB After Sales, see Chapter 9.1.3 Contact information for Motors and Generators Service.

results.question: When an ABB machine is first switched on for a trial run, how briefly should it be kept energized?
results.source: §5.6.3, p.64 (source text says 'first start', not 'switched on'/'energized')
results.rewritten_query: ABB machine initial trial run: recommended maximum duration to keep the machine energized during first power-on.
results.answer: For the first trial run, keep the ABB machine energized for **about one second**. This verifies the direction of rotation and confirms that rotating parts do not contact stationary parts. [3]

contexts:
[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 65 · 5.7.1 Supervision during the first run
During running the machine the first time, it is verified that the machine functions as expected. The vibration level, the temperature of the windings and bearings, and other equipment are monitored frequently. If the machine functions as expected, the machine can be left running for a longer time.
Check the operating load of the machine by comparing the load current with the value given on the rating plate of the machine.
Record the temperature readings given by the temperature detectors placed in the windings and possibly in the bearings. Check the temperatures frequently to ensure that they remain below the limits. Continuous temperature monitoring is recommended.
NOTE:
If resistance temperature detector (RTD, Pt-100) or equivalent is not available, the surface temperature of the bearing area shall, if possible, be measured. The bearing temperature is approximately 10°C (20°F) higher than the surface temperature.
In case of any deviations from expected normal operation, e.g. elevated temperatures, noise or vibration, shut down the machine, and find the reason for the deviations. If necessary, consult the manufacturer of the machine.
NOTE:
Do not disengage any protective devices during running of the machine, or during search for a reason for unexpected function of the machine.

[2] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 69 · 6.3 Number of starts
The number of allowed consecutive starts of direct on line supplied machines depends essentially on the load characteristics (torque curve vs. rotational speed, inertia), and on the machine type and design. Too many and/or too heavy starts cause abnormally high temperatures and stresses on the machine, thus accelerating the ageing of the machine and resulting in an abnormally short lifetime, or even a machine failure.
For information on the allowed consecutive or annual starts, please see the performance data sheet or consult the manufacturer. The load characteristics of the application are needed for determining the starting frequency. As a guideline, the maximum number of starts in a typical application is 1000 starts per year.
A counter system for controlling the number of starts should be used and maintenance intervals should be determined based on equivalent operating hours, see Chapter 7.3 Maintenance program.
NOTE:

[3] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 64 · 5.6.3 Starting
The first start should last only about one (1) second, during which the direction of rotation of the machine is verified. The direction of rotation of possible external blower motors must also be verified. It is also verified that the rotating parts do not touch any stationary parts.
NOTE:
If the machine does not have an axially locating bearing, and the machine is started uncoupled, it is normal that the shaft will move axially before stabilizing.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 74 · 7.3 Maintenance program
This chapter presents a recommended maintenance program for ABB machines. This maintenance program is of a general nature, and should be considered as a minimum level of maintenance. Maintenance should be intensified when local conditions are demanding or very high reliability is required. It should also be noted that even when following this maintenance program, normal supervision and observation of the machine's condition is required.
Please note that even though the maintenance programs below have been customized to match the machine, it might contain references to accessories not available on all machines.
The maintenance program is based on four levels of maintenance, which rotate according to operating hours. The amount of work and down time vary, so that level 1 includes mainly quick visual inspections and level 4 more demanding measurements and replacements. More information about the spare part packages suitable for these maintenances can be found in Chapter 9.2 Spare parts for rotating electrical machines. The recommended maintenance interval can be seen in Table 6 Maintenance intervals. The operation hour recommendation in this chapter is given as equivalent operating hours (Eq. h), that can be counted by the following formula:

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 56 · 4.3.3 Insulation resistance measurements
Before a machine is started up for the first time, after a long period of standstill or within the scope of general maintenance work, the insulation resistance of the machine must be measured, see Chapter 7.6.4 Insulation resistance test.

results.question: What symptoms suggest a faulty temperature sensor in the winding or bearing of an ABB machine?
results.source: §8.3.2, p.114 (source text says 'Pt-100 detector', not 'temperature sensor')
results.expected_answer: infinite or zero resistance; disappearance of measurement signal during/after startup; a significantly different resistance value in a single detector
results.rewritten_query: Symptoms indicating a faulty winding or bearing temperature sensor in an ABB electric machine.
results.answer:
## Symptoms and likely indication

A **high winding-temperature indication** with no confirmed corresponding machine problem may suggest a faulty temperature measurement system, sensor, or wiring; the prescribed check is to verify the measurements, sensors, and wiring. [1][2][3]

| Symptom | Possible cause | Check or corrective action |
|---|---|---|
| High winding temperature | Faulty instrumentation or measurement system | Check measurements, sensors, and wiring. [1][2][3] |
| High winding temperature | Winding fault | Check the windings. [1][2][3] |

ABB machines have stator-winding Pt-100 temperature detectors inside the stator-core slots; these detectors cannot be replaced directly. Spare Pt-100 detectors may be used if the primary detector fails, including during operation. [4]

## Procedure

1. Check the indicated temperature measurement, the sensor, and its wiring. [1][2][3]
2. If the primary stator Pt-100 detector has failed, use the installed spare Pt-100 detector as the replacement where available. [4]
3. If the spare Pt-100 also fails, the stated corrective action is to add Pt-100 elements into the stator-winding end. [4]
4. Have the checks and corrective actions performed by qualified personnel; contact ABB Motors and Generators Service if in doubt. [5]

The supplied context does **not** identify specific symptoms, temperature values, limits, or diagnostic criteria for a faulty **bearing** temperature sensor; it only directs the reader to the lubrication-system and bearings chapter for high bearing temperatures. [1][2][3]

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 118 · 9.2.3 Need of spare parts
Other types of wear occur due to elevated temperatures, electrical disturbances and chemical reactions.
Air filters, which protect the machine interior from contamination, become themselves saturated with air impurities and need to be replaced to ensure the correct operation of the cooling unit, and the continuous protection of sensitive machine parts.
The electrical windings of the ABB machines have good protection against wear, but only if correct maintenance and operating conditions are followed. The correct operating temperature must not be exceeded and the windings must be cleaned from dirt regularly. The winding can also be subjected to accelerated wear due to a number of electrical disturbances.
There are stator winding Pt-100 temperature detectors located inside the stator core slots, which cannot be replaced. Therefore, the ABB practice is to add spare Pt-100 detectors in the stator core. These detectors are not to be considered as regular spare parts because they are intended to be used as a replacement in case of a stator Pt-100 element failure during commissioning. However, these elements can be taken into use also during operation if the primary detector fails. If the spare element should fail, the possible corrective action is to add Pt-100 elements into the stator winding end.

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 101 · 8.1 Trouble shooting
This chapter is intended as a help in the event of an operational failure with an ABB delivered rotating electrical machine. The trouble shooting charts given below can aid in locating and repairing mechanical, electrical and thermal problems, and problems associated with the lubrication system. The checks and corrective actions mentioned should always be conducted by qualified personnel. If in any doubt, the Motors and Generators Service of ABB should be contacted for more information or technical assistance regarding trouble shooting and maintenance.

results.question: What megohm-meter voltage should be applied when megger-testing the main stator windings of an ABB machine?
results.source: §7.6.4.4, p.91 (source text says 'insulation resistance test', not 'megger'/'megohm-meter')
results.rewritten_query: Recommended megohmmeter test voltage for the main stator windings of an ABB electric machine.
results.answer:
## Required megger voltage

Apply **1000 VDC** to the main stator windings. The specified test duration is **1 minute**, after which record the insulation-resistance value. [5]

## Test procedure

1. Disconnect all power-supply cables. [5]
2. Ensure the current-transformer secondary connections, including spare cores, are not open. [5]
3. Earth the machine frame and any stator windings not being tested. [5]
4. Measure the winding temperature and earth all resistance-temperature detectors. [5]
5. Remove any earthing of voltage transformers, if present. [5]
6. Perform the measurement in the terminal box, normally between the machine frame and the complete stator winding group, with the three phases still connected at the neutral point. [5]

![Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements](diagrams/fdb5c8bb-ba46-40f5-b9a2-e30841e3a2b4/fig39_1.png)

7. If the complete winding gives a low value and the phases can be disconnected, test each phase separately with the frame and the two untested phases earthed. [5]
8. After testing, briefly earth the winding phases to discharge them. [5]

The supplied context does not specify a minimum acceptable insulation-resistance value.

[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 94 · 7.6.5 Insulation resistance measurement for auxiliaries
To ensure correct operation of the machines protections and other auxiliaries, their condition can be determined by an insulation resistance test. The procedure is described in detail in Chapter 7.6 Maintenance of stator and rotor windings. The test voltage for the space heater should be 500 VDC and for other auxiliaries 100 VDC. The insulation resistance measurement for Pt-100 detectors or proximity probes is not recommended.

[2] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 93 · 7.6.4.5 Rotor winding insulation resistance measurement
The insulation resistance of the rotor winding is measured with an insulation resistance meter. The test voltage of the rotor windings should be 1000 VDC. Required notes and measures:
- Verify that all power supply cables are disconnected from the main supply.
- Verify the slip ring unit connection cables are disconnected from their supply.
- Verify that the frame of the machine and the stator windings are earthed.
- The shaft is earthed.
- The rotor winding phases not been tested are earthed. The rotor winding can be internally connected in a delta or star connection. If this is the case, it is not possible to measure the phases individually.
- The carbon brush connections are checked to be in good order.
- The measurement device is checked.
- The stator winding temperatures are measured, and considered as a reference value for the rotor winding temperature.
The insulation resistance meter is connected between the whole rotor winding and the shaft of the machine, see Figure 40 Insulation resistance measurement of the rotor winding. After performed rotor winding measurements, the rotor winding phases must be briefly earthed in order to discharge the windings.
Figure 40 Insulation resistance measurement of the rotor winding
In the figure above the rotor is star-connected.

[3] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 89 · 7.6 Maintenance of stator and rotor windings
The windings of rotating electrical machines are subjected to electrical, mechanical and thermal stresses. The windings and insulation gradually age and deteriorate due to these stresses. Therefore, the service life of the machine often depends on the insulation durability.
Many processes leading to damages can be prevented or at least slowed down with appropriate maintenance and regular testing. This chapter offers a general description on how to perform basic maintenance and tests.
In many countries, ABB Service offers complete service maintenance packages, which include comprehensive testing.
Before conducting any maintenance work on the electrical windings, general electrical safety precautions are to be taken and local regulations are to be respected in order to prevent personnel accidents. See Chapter 7.2 Safety precautions for more information.
Independent test and maintenance instructions can also be found in the following international standards:
1. IEEE Std. 43-2000, IEEE Recommended Practice for Testing Insulation Resistance of Rotating Machines
2. IEEE Std. 432-1992, IEEE Guide for Insulation Maintenance for Rotating Electrical Machinery (5 hp to Less Than 10 000 hp).

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 99 · Following note for rotor type: Permanent magnet
NOTE:
When disassembling the permanent magnet synchronous machine, always contact ABB Motors and Generators Service for more instructions.
-

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 92 · 7.6.4.4 Stator winding insulation resistance measurement
The insulation resistance is measured using an insulation resistance meter. The test voltage is 1000 VDC. The test time is 1 minute, after which the insulation resistance value is recorded. Before the insulation resistance test is conducted, the following actions must be taken:
- Check that the secondary connections of the current transformers (CT's), including spare cores are not open. See Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
- Verify that all power supply cables are disconnected.
- Verify that the frame of the machine and the stator windings not being tested are earthed.
- The winding temperature is measured.
- All resistance temperature detectors are earthed.
- Possible earthing of voltage transformers (not common) must be removed.
The insulation resistance measuring should be carried out in the terminal box. The test is usually performed to the whole winding as a group, in which case the meter is connected between the frame of the machine and the winding; See Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements. The frame is earthed and the three phases of the stator winding remain connected at the neutral point, see Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
If the measured insulation resistance of the whole winding is lower than specified, and the phase windings can easily be disconnected from each other, each phase can also be measured separately. This is not possible for all machines. In this measurement, the tester is connected between the frame of the machine and one of the windings. The frame and the two phases not measured are earthed; see Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
Carbon dust on slip rings and naked copper surfaces lower the insulation resistance values of the rotor.
When phases are measured separately, all star-points of the winding system must be removed. If the star-point of the component cannot be removed, as in a typical tri-phase voltage transformer, the whole component must be removed.
Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements
- a) Insulation resistance measurement for star connected winding.
- b) Insulation resistance measurement for delta connected winding.
- c) Insulation resistance measurement for one phase of the winding. The 'MΩ' represents the insulation resistance meter.
After the insulation resistance measurement the winding phases must be earthed briefly in order to discharge them.

results.question: How tightly, in Nm, must an oiled M10 bolt of property class 8.8 be fastened on an ABB machine?
results.source: Table 7, p.79 (source uses 'tightening torque', not 'how tightly fastened')
results.rewritten_query: Required tightening torque in Nm for an oiled M10 property class 8.8 bolt on an ABB machine.
results.answer:
## Required tightening torque

An oiled **M10 bolt, property class 8.8, on an ABB machine** should be tightened to **44 Nm**. [1]

| Bolt size | Condition | Property class | Tightening torque |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| M10 | Oiled | 8.8 | **44 Nm** [1] |

## Application and procedure

1. Confirm that the fastener is an **M10**, property class **8.8** bolt. [1]
2. Confirm that the bolt is being installed **oiled**, not dry; the ABB value for a dry M10 bolt is **46 Nm**. [1]
3. Tighten the bolt to **44 Nm** using the applicable torque tool. [1]
4. Verify that the fastener is not part of an excluded application, such as diodes, support insulators, bearings, cable terminals, pole fastenings, bus-bar terminals, surge arrestors, capacitors, current transformers, rectifier or thyristor bridges, or another location where the manual specifies a different value. [1]
5. Verify fastener tightness regularly, with particular attention to grouting, anchor bolts, and rotor parts. [1]

results.question: How is the debris screen on the slip ring housing of an ABB machine cleaned?
results.source: §7.7.3, p.96 (source says 'carbon dust filter', not 'debris screen')
results.rewritten_query: Cleaning procedure for the debris screen on the slip-ring housing of an ABB electric machine.
results.answer:
## Cleaning method

If the “debris screen” refers to the slip-ring housing’s carbon-dust filter, clean it by **washing, beating, or spraying**. [1]

1. Inspect the filter manually at frequent intervals. [1]
2. Clean the filter using washing, beating, or spraying. [1]
3. If the differential-pressure switch gives an alarm, change the filter immediately rather than merely cleaning it. [1]
4. Use the brush-wear-based interval shown in Figure 42 to determine the maximum cleaning interval. [1]

The provided context does not specify the washing medium, spray pressure, beating method, or numerical cleaning-interval limits from Figure 42.

[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 96 · 7.7.3 Care of carbon dust filter
The slip ring unit of the permanent contact type is equipped with filter for carbon dust. The cleaning interval of the filter in respect to carbon brush wear is shown in Figure 42 Maximum cleaning interval of the slip ring housing carbon dust filter, parameter brush wear in mm/10³ h.
The slip ring housing is equipped with a differential pressure switch for monitoring the condition of the filters. The filter must be changed immediately after an alarm. It is also highly recommended that the operating personnel manually inspects the filters frequently.
The carbon dust filter can be cleaned by washing, beating, or spraying.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 97 · 7.7.4.4 Movability of the short circuit ring
It must be checked at regular intervals, that the short circuit ring bushing can easily move on its sliding surface (rotor shaft). Sliding surface must be cleaned from dirt and excessive carbon dust. The sliding surfaces can be greased when needed by applying a thin film of Teflon lubricant, for example Interflon Paste HT1200 Spray from Interflon.

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 95 · 7.7.1.1 Standstill period
When a longer standstill period for the machine begins, the brushes should be lifted up. During transport, storage, installation or longer interruptions, the sliding surfaces of the slip-rings might be tarnished or covered with dirt, etc. Before restarting the machine, the sliding surfaces should be inspected and cleaned.

results.question: At what oscillation speed does the alarm trigger for a rigidly mounted ABB bearing housing?
results.rewritten_query: What oscillation speed triggers the alarm for a rigidly mounted ABB bearing housing?
results.answer:
## ABB rigidly mounted bearing housing

The **initial alarm triggers at 3.4 mm/s RMS vibration velocity** for a rigid support. The corresponding trip value is **7.1 mm/s RMS**. [1]

| Support class | Initial alarm | Trip |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rigid | 3.4 mm/s RMS [1] | 7.1 mm/s RMS [1] |

These are initial standard values; after establishing the machine’s steady-state on-site baseline, the alarm setting should be adjusted accordingly. [1]

### Maintenance response

1. Monitor the vibration of the driving–driven machine system. [3]
2. If vibration reaches or exceeds the alarm level, check the bearing condition, lubrication amount and quality, regreasing interval, coupling, mounting, and alignment. [4]
3. Check for damaged bearing parts, bearing currents, faulty seals, incorrect assembly, foreign matter, or a complete bearing failure. [4]
4. Investigate and correct the cause before relying on the trip threshold; the ABB table identifies **7.1 mm/s RMS** as the rigid-support trip value. [1]

[2] Nidec Motor Manual, p. 39 · Limits of Bearing Housing Vibration
Question: Please explain the limits of bearing housing vibration.
Answer: The following limits of vibration pertain to uncoupled, resiliently mounted machines, running at no load. For machines tested with rigid mounting, the values given should be multiplied by 0.8. Vibration levels given here refer to internally excited vibration only. Motors as installed (in situ) may exhibit higher levels.
Figures 10a and 10b, taken from NEMA MG17.08, show limits for bearing housing vibration levels of machines resiliently mounted for both unfiltered and filtered measurements.
For unfiltered vibration, the measured velocity level shall not exceed the limit for the appropriate curve in figure 10a corresponding to the rotational frequency. For filtered vibration, the velocity level at each component frequency of the spectrum analysis shall not exceed the value for the appropriate curve in figure 10a at that frequency.

results.question: What is the exact re-greasing interval, in hours, for the rolling bearings of an ABB machine?
results.expected_answer: No universal number — the interval is found on the bearing plate (machine-specific); regardless, re-greasing must occur at least once per year, and the interval halves per 15°C rise above the 70°C baseline
results.rewritten_query: ABB machine rolling-bearing re-greasing interval, specified in operating hours.
results.answer:
## Answer

The exact re-greasing interval in operating hours **cannot be determined from the supplied context**. It is specified on the machine’s bearing plate. The interval must not exceed 12 months, regardless of the stated interval. [1][5]

The interval shown on the bearing plate is based on a bearing operating temperature of 70°C (160°F). [1]

- For every 15°C (30°F) increase in bearing temperature, the re-greasing interval should be halved. [1]
- For every 15°C (30°F) decrease, the interval may be doubled. [1]
- Higher operating temperature shortens the interval. [1]
- The 8,000- and 20,000-hour values in the context are recommended **oil-change** intervals for mineral-oil-lubricated bearings, not grease re-greasing intervals. [4]

## Re-greasing procedure

1. Verify that the grease is suitable for the machine. [2]
2. Clean the grease nipples and the surrounding area. [2]
3. Verify that the lubrication channel is open; open its handle if fitted. [2]
4. Inject the specified amount and type of grease into the bearing. [2]
5. Allow the machine to run for 1–2 hours so excess grease is forced out; the bearing temperature may temporarily rise. [2]
6. Close the lubrication-channel handle if fitted. [2]

Beware of rotating parts during re-greasing, and follow the grease manufacturer’s safety precautions because grease can irritate skin and inflame the eyes. [2][3]

[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · 7.5.3.3 Re-greasing intervals
Rolling bearings of electrical machines need to be re-greased at regular intervals. The re-greasing interval is found on the bearing plate.
NOTE:
Regardless of the re-greasing interval, the bearings need to be re-greased at least once per year.
The re-greasing intervals are calculated for an operating temperature of 70°C (160°F). If the operating temperature is lower or higher than the assumed, the re-grease interval has to be altered accordingly. Higher operating temperature decreases the re-greasing interval.
NOTE:
An increase in the ambient temperature raises the temperature of the bearings correspondingly. The values for the re-greasing interval should be halved for every 15°C (30°F) increase in bearing temperature and may be once doubled for a 15°C (30°F) decrease in bearing temperature.

[2] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · Manual re-greasing while the machine is running
Re-greasing while the machine is running:
- Verify that the grease to be used is suitable.
- Clean the grease nipples and the area around them.
- Verify that the lubrication channel is open, if equipped with a handle, open it.
- Press the specified amount and type of grease into the bearing.
- Let the machine run 1-2 hours in order to ensure that all excess grease is forced out of the bearing. The bearing temperature may temporarily increase during this time.
- If equipped with a handle, close it.
NOTE:
Beware of all rotating parts during the re-greasing.

[3] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · 7.5.3.4 Re-greasing
All rolling bearings of rotating electrical machines need to be re-greased, see Chapter 7.5.3.3 Re-greasing intervals. The re-greasing can be performed either manually or by means of an automatic system. In either case, it has to be verified that a suitable amount of the correct grease is entering the bearing at suitable intervals.
NOTE:
Grease can cause skin irritation and eye inflammation. Follow all safety precautions specified by the grease manufacturer.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 84 · 7.5.2.5 Oil change schedule for mineral oils
For self-lubricated bearings cleaning intervals with oil changes of approximately 8000 operating hours are recommended and approx. 20000 operating hours for bearings with oil circulation systems.
Shorter oil change intervals may be necessary in case of frequent start-ups, high oil temperatures or excessively high contamination due to external influences.
The correct oil change interval can be found on the bearing plate and dimensional drawing, see Chapter 2.1.2 Bearing plate.
Following chapter for bearing type: Rolling bearing

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 66 · Figure 32 Example of lubrication channel through bearing arrangement of horizontal machine
NOTE:
NOTE:
Start-up greasing may take several grease portions (3-10 times amount mentioned at the lubrication plate).
The re-lubrication interval will never be longer than 12 months.
The type of original grease used is found on the bearing plate on the machine. Acceptable types of grease can be found in Chapter 7.5.3 Rolling bearings.
NOTE:
Do not mix greases! There must be only one type of grease inside the bearing - not mixture of two or more greases.
The temperature of the bearings will initially increase because of the excess grease. After few hours, the excess grease will be discharged through the lubrication valve and the temperature of the bearing will return to normal running temperature.
If available, and after the machine has been running for several hours, measure the vibrations or SPM-values from the SPM-nipples, and record the values for future reference use.

results.question: What is the maximum permissible shaft key length for an ABB HXR induction motor?
results.rewritten_query: Maximum permissible shaft key length for an ABB HXR induction motor.
results.answer:
## Answer

The maximum permissible shaft key length for an ABB HXR induction motor **cannot be determined from the provided context**.

The context identifies HXR induction machines as covered models, including sizes 315 to 560 for dust-ignition protection and increased-safety applications, but it gives no shaft-key length limit. [1][3]

The thermal-expansion information provides a rotor expansion calculation based on frame length, but it does not specify shaft-key dimensions or permissible key length. [2]

The only shaft-key-related entry is a blank Siemens service-record field for “Keyway”; it contains no dimensions and does not establish an ABB HXR limit. [5]

A definitive value would require the applicable ABB motor dimension drawing, shaft/keyway drawing, or motor-specific technical documentation.

[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · 7.5.3.3 Re-greasing intervals
Rolling bearings of electrical machines need to be re-greased at regular intervals. The re-greasing interval is found on the bearing plate.
NOTE:
Regardless of the re-greasing interval, the bearings need to be re-greased at least once per year.
The re-greasing intervals are calculated for an operating temperature of 70°C (160°F). If the operating temperature is lower or higher than the assumed, the re-grease interval has to be altered accordingly. Higher operating temperature decreases the re-greasing interval.
NOTE:
An increase in the ambient temperature raises the temperature of the bearings correspondingly. The values for the re-greasing interval should be halved for every 15°C (30°F) increase in bearing temperature and may be once doubled for a 15°C (30°F) decrease in bearing temperature.

It is essential to use grease of good quality and with the correct base soap. This will ensure a long and trouble free lifetime of the bearings.
Grease used for re-greasing should have the following properties:
- Be special rolling bearing grease.
- Be of good quality with a lithium complex soap, and with mineral-, or PAO-oil.
- Have a base oil viscosity of 100 to 160 cSt at 40°C (105°F).
- Have a consistency NLGI grade between 1.5 and 3. For vertically or in hot conditions mounted machines, NLGI grade 2 or 3 is recommended.
- Have a continuous temperature range between -30°C (-20°F) and at least +120°C (250°F).
Grease with the correct properties is available from all major lubricant manufacturers. If the make of grease is changed and compatibility is uncertain, consult the manufacturing ABB factory, see Chapter 9.1.3 Contact information for Motors and Generators Service.
| NOTE: | Do not mix greases! There must be only one type of grease inside the bearing - not a mixture of two or more greases. |
| - | - |
| NOTE: | Grease additives are recommended. However, a written guarantee should be obtained from the lubricant manufacturer stating that the additives do not damage the bearings or the properties of the grease in the field of the operating temperature. This is especially important for EP additives. |
| NOTE: | Lubricants containing EP admixtures are not recommended. |

results.question: What one-minute insulation resistance should a Siemens vertical motor with MICLAD VPI insulation exceed?
results.expected_answer: Greater than 1000 megohms after one minute (values above 5000 megohms are common)
results.rewritten_query: What minimum one-minute insulation resistance should a Siemens vertical motor with MICLAD VPI insulation have?
results.answer:
## Required value

A Siemens vertical motor with MICLAD™ VPI insulation should have a **one-minute insulation resistance greater than 1000 MΩ**. Values above 5000 MΩ are common. [1]

## Test conditions and procedure

1. Check the insulation resistance before connecting the motor to the power supply. [2]
2. Use a hand-cranked or solid-state insulation-resistance tester at **at least 500 V**, but do not exceed the motor’s rated voltage. [1][2]
3. Record the resistance after the test voltage has been applied for **one minute** and verify that it exceeds **1000 MΩ**. [1]
4. If the stator is cleaned, measure insulation resistance both before and after cleaning. [3]

Low resistance may be caused by excess humidity or dirt even when the actual insulation remains intact. [4]

[1] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 18 · Insulation Resistance
Check insulation resistance periodically. Use a hand cranked or solid state insulation resistance tester and test with at least 500 volts, but not greater than motor rated voltage.
For motors with newer insulation systems such as MICLAD™ VPI, the insulation resistance after one minute should be greater than 1000 megohms. (Values in excess of 5000 megohms are common.) For older motors, the minimum value recommended in IEEE Standard 43 can be used. The value in megohms, when corrected to 40°C, is equal to the motor rated voltage in kilovolts plus 1. For example, for a motor with a rated voltage of 2300 volts, the limit value would be:
2.3 + 1 = 3.3 (megohms).

[2] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 10 · Insulation Resistance
Check insulation resistance prior to connecting motor to power supply. A hand cranked or solid state electronic insulation resistance tester, at least 500 volts d.c., but not over rated voltage, is usually used (see Maintenance).
See IEEE Recommended Practice for Testing Insulation Resistance Rotating Machinery IEEE Std 43.

[3] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 18 · Stator Cleaning
MICLAD™ form wound VPI (vacuum pressure impregnated) insulated coils may be cleaned with a quick drying solvent and lint free cloths or steam cleaned with low-pressure steam, then the entire stator oven baked at 200°F for 12 hours and then 230°F for 12 hours.
The stator winding insulation resistance should be measured before and after any cleaning operation.
The windings may be cleaned with a solvent compatible with the insulation system and oven dried. Water and detergents with an oven drying cycle may be used as an alternate on MICLAD™ VPI insulation systems.
MICLAD™ is a Siemens trademark.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 92 · 7.6.4.3 Minimum values for insulation resistance
Criteria for windings in a normal condition:
Generally, the insulation resistance values for dry windings should exceed the minimum values significantly. Definite values are impossible to give, because resistance varies depending on the machine type and local conditions. In addition, the insulation resistance is affected by the age and usage of the machine. Therefore, the following values can only be considered as guidelines.
The insulation resistance limits, which are given below, are valid at 40 °C, and when the test voltage has been applied for 1 minute or longer.
- Rotor.
For induction machines with wound rotors: R(1-10 min at 40 °C) > 5 MΩ.
NOTE:
- Stator.
For new stators: R(1-10 min at 40 °C) > 1000 MΩ. If the measuring conditions are extremely warm and humid, R(1-10 min at 40 °C) values above 100 MΩ can be accepted.
For used stators: R(1-10 min at 40 °C) > 100 MΩ.
NOTE:
If the values given here are not reached, the reason for the low insulation resistance should be determined. A low insulation resistance value is often caused by excess humidity or dirt, although the actual insulation is intact.

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 36 · 3.3.1 Insulation resistance measurements
Before a machine is started up for the first time, after a long period of standstill or within the scope of general maintenance work, the insulation resistance of the machine must be measured. This includes measuring the stature winding and all auxiliary devices. For machines equipped with slip ring, the measuring also includes the rotor winding, see Chapter 7.6.4 Insulation resistance test.

results.question: How should a Toshiba TM21 motor be prepared for long-term storage?
results.rewritten_query: Toshiba TM21 motor long-term storage preparation and preservation procedures.
results.answer:
## Conclusion

The provided context is insufficient to define a Toshiba TM21–specific long-term-storage preparation procedure. It contains Siemens and Nidec guidance, but no Toshiba TM21 storage instructions, storage-environment requirements, lubrication details, or insulation-resistance limits.

## Conditions identified in the context

- For a motor out of service or in storage for more than 30 days, consult the applicable storage recommendations before returning it to service. [1]
- For storage periods of three months or longer, or where climate variations occur, consult the applicable storage recommendations. [2]
- Storage maintenance should be documented for warranty purposes. [2]

## Checks before returning the motor to service

The following is post-storage guidance in the supplied context, not a confirmed Toshiba TM21 storage procedure:

1. Relubricate the bearings as applicable. [3][4]
2. Remove desiccant, if present. [3]
3. Inspect the motor externally to confirm it is clean, ventilation openings are unobstructed, and no damage has occurred. [4]
4. Test the motor-winding insulation resistance with a megohmmeter. [3][4]
5. Rotate the shaft and check for bearing roughness or interference between rotating and stationary parts. [4]
6. Perform a bench test for excessive current draw, noise, or vibration. [4]
7. Have an authorized service station correct any deficiencies and install a tag or plate showing the inspection date. [4]

results.question: What vibration alarm limit does GE Vernova specify for its vertical induction motors?
results.rewritten_query: GE Vernova vertical induction motor vibration alarm limit specifications
results.answer:
## Answer

The provided context does **not specify a vibration alarm limit for GE Vernova vertical induction motors**, so a GE Vernova-specific value cannot be determined from the supplied material.

The context contains these limits from other manufacturers:

| Source and condition | Alarm limit | Trip limit |
|---|---:|---:|
| Siemens vertical motor, shaft vibration at 3600 RPM, peak-to-peak | 2.8 mils | 3.3 mils [4] |
| Siemens vertical motor, shaft vibration at 1800 RPM, peak-to-peak | 3.2 mils | 3.7 mils [4] |
| Siemens vertical motor, shaft vibration at 1200 RPM, peak-to-peak | 3.8 mils | 4.3 mils [4] |
| Siemens vertical motor, shaft vibration at 900 RPM and slower, peak-to-peak | 4.5 mils | 5.0 mils [4] |
| ABB bearing-housing vibration, rigid support, RMS velocity | 3.4 mm/s | 7.1 mm/s [3] |
| ABB bearing-housing vibration, flexible support, RMS velocity | 5.3 mm/s | 11.0 mm/s [3] |

These values should not be presented as GE Vernova limits because the context identifies them as Siemens or ABB values. [3][4]

## Available diagnostic procedure

1. Run the vertical motor at minimum load and check vibration. [2]
2. If vibration is excessive, loosen the flange mounting bolts and shift the motor within the mounting-flange clearance. [2]
3. If this does not reduce vibration to the acceptable limit, check shaft alignment and system reed frequency when the motor is coupled to the load. [2]

A GE Vernova-specific alarm value, measurement location, vibration quantity, and acceptance procedure would require documentation not included in the context.

## Answer

The provided context does not specify Siemens alarm and trip temperatures for a **sleeve bearing** on a vertical induction motor.

results.question: What is the NEMA MG1 unfiltered vibration limit for a resiliently mounted Siemens vertical motor running at 900 RPM?
results.rewritten_query: NEMA MG 1 unfiltered vibration limit for a resiliently mounted Siemens vertical motor operating at 900 RPM.
results.answer:
## Limit

The NEMA MG1 unfiltered vibration limit for a resiliently mounted Siemens vertical motor running at **900 RPM** is **0.12 in/s peak (3.0 mm/s)**. [1]

| Speed, RPM | Rotational frequency | Unfiltered velocity limit |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 900 | 15 Hz | 0.12 in/s peak (3.0 mm/s) [1][4] |

## Conditions and procedure

This limit applies to the standard unfiltered vibration measurement for a resiliently mounted motor. [1][2]

1. After tightening the flange mounting bolts, check the motor end play. [1]
2. Run the unit at minimum load and check vibration. [1]
3. If vibration exceeds the limit, loosen the flange mounting bolts and shift the motor within the mounting-flange clearance. [1]
4. If shifting does not reduce vibration to the acceptable limit and the motor is coupled to the load, check shaft alignment and the system reed frequency. [1]

Follow the manufacturer's instructions when mounting or removing couplings or other drive elements and cover them with a touch guard. For trial run in uncoupled state, lock or remove the shaft end key. Avoid excessive radial and axial bearing loads (note manufacturer's documentation). The balance of the machine is indicated as H = Half and F = Full key. In half key cases coupling must be half key balanced. In full key cases coupling must be balanced without a key. In case of protruding, visible part of the shaft end key, establish mechanical balance.

If there are any conflicts between these safety instructions and the user manual, these safety instructions prevail.

These instructions present general recommendations for installation, operation and maintenance of induction motors built at the Norwood plant. If additional information is required, contact Siemens Energy & Automation.

Criteria for windings in a normal condition:
Generally, the insulation resistance values for dry windings should exceed the minimum values significantly. In addition, the insulation resistance is affected by the age and usage of the machine. Therefore, the following values can only be considered as guidelines.

results.question: What minimum insulation resistance does Siemens recommend for an older vertical motor rated 2300 V?
results.expected_answer: 3.3 MΩ corrected to 40°C (rated kV + 1, per IEEE Std 43); MICLAD VPI motors should exceed 1000 MΩ after one minute
results.rewritten_query: Siemens minimum recommended winding insulation resistance for an older 2300 V vertical motor.
results.answer:
## Minimum value

For an older Siemens vertical motor rated at **2300 V**, the minimum recommended insulation resistance is **3.3 MΩ, corrected to 40 °C**. [1]

$$
R_{\min} = 2.3\ \text{kV} + 1 = 3.3\ \text{M}\Omega
$$

## Recommended checks and procedure

1. **Test the motor before connecting it to the power supply.** [2]

2. **Use a hand-cranked or solid-state insulation-resistance tester with a test voltage of at least 500 V and no greater than the motor’s rated voltage.** [1][2]

3. **Measure the winding temperature and correct the measured insulation resistance to 40 °C before comparing it with the 3.3 MΩ limit.** [1][3]

4. **If the measured value is below the limit, investigate the cause rather than assuming the insulation itself has failed.** [3]

Likely causes of a low reading include:

- Excess humidity. [3]
- Dirt or contamination. [3]
- The age and usage history of the machine. [3]

Check insulation resistance prior to connecting motor to power supply. A hand cranked or solid state electronic insulation resistance tester, at least 500 volts d.c., but not over rated voltage, is usually used (see Maintenance).
See IEEE Recommended Practice for Testing Insulation Resistance Rotating Machinery IEEE Std 43.

Criteria for windings in a normal condition:
Generally, the insulation resistance values for dry windings should exceed the minimum values significantly. Definite values are impossible to give, because resistance varies depending on the machine type and local conditions. - Rotor.

NOTE:
- Stator.

For used stators: R(1-10 min at 40 °C) > 100 MΩ.
NOTE:
If the values given here are not reached, the reason for the low insulation resistance should be determined. A low insulation resistance value is often caused by excess humidity or dirt, although the actual insulation is intact.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 94 · 7.6.5 Insulation resistance measurement for auxiliaries
To ensure correct operation of the machines protections and other auxiliaries, their condition can be determined by an insulation resistance test. The procedure is described in detail in Chapter 7.6 Maintenance of stator and rotor windings. The test voltage for the space heater should be 500 VDC and for other auxiliaries 100 VDC. The insulation resistance measurement for Pt-100 detectors or proximity probes is not recommended.

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 92 · 7.6.4.4 Stator winding insulation resistance measurement
The insulation resistance is measured using an insulation resistance meter. The test voltage is 1000 VDC. The test time is 1 minute, after which the insulation resistance value is recorded. Before the insulation resistance test is conducted, the following actions must be taken:
- Check that the secondary connections of the current transformers (CT's), including spare cores are not open. See Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
- Verify that all power supply cables are disconnected.
- Verify that the frame of the machine and the stator windings not being tested are earthed.
- The winding temperature is measured.
- All resistance temperature detectors are earthed.
- Possible earthing of voltage transformers (not common) must be removed.
The insulation resistance measuring should be carried out in the terminal box. The test is usually performed to the whole winding as a group, in which case the meter is connected between the frame of the machine and the winding; See Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements. The frame is earthed and the three phases of the stator winding remain connected at the neutral point, see Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
If the measured insulation resistance of the whole winding is lower than specified, and the phase windings can easily be disconnected from each other, each phase can also be measured separately. This is not possible for all machines. In this measurement, the tester is connected between the frame of the machine and one of the windings. The frame and the two phases not measured are earthed; see Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements.
Carbon dust on slip rings and naked copper surfaces lower the insulation resistance values of the rotor.
When phases are measured separately, all star-points of the winding system must be removed. If the star-point of the component cannot be removed, as in a typical tri-phase voltage transformer, the whole component must be removed.
Figure 39 Connections of the stator windings for insulation resistance measurements
- a) Insulation resistance measurement for star connected winding.
- b) Insulation resistance measurement for delta connected winding.
- c) Insulation resistance measurement for one phase of the winding. The 'MΩ' represents the insulation resistance meter.
After the insulation resistance measurement the winding phases must be earthed briefly in order to discharge them.

contexts:
[1] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 23 · Lower Guide Bearing
The function of the lower guide bearing with a Kingsbury-type bearing is to provide radial location of the shaft with no thrust or end play limit. This bearing may be one of three types - grease-lubricated ball bearing, oil-lubricated ball bearing, or oil-lubricated sleeve bearing (See Figures 9, 10 and 11).

[2] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 23 · Thrust Bearing
Principle elements of the Kingsbury-type thrust bearing are the rotating thrust runner and the stationary pivotal thrust shoes (See Figure 7) The runner is the highly polished bottom surface of the thrust block and receives the thrust load through a massive nut above the thrust block threaded on the top end of the shaft. The pivotal thrust shoes are faced with tin-hard Babbitt and machined to form an accurate surface plate.
During operation, the thrust bearing revolves in an oil bath which covers the bearing. Each shoe is free to tilt slightly in any direction and sets itself by pivoting at a minute angle causing a wedge-shaped film of oil to form between the shoe and the runner. An end play of 0.012 - 0.017 inches is preset at the factory by shims between the thrust plate and the upper guide (upthrust) bearing.

[3] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 22 · End Play
Machines designed for applications involving primarily continuous heavy downthrust but having momentary upthrust are equipped with angular contact or spherical roller bearings. Spherical roller bearings may be preloaded with springs (See Figure 8). The end play is most often 0.005 to 0.008 in. but see the motor outline for the exact value for your motor. The bottom bearing takes the momentary upthrust and prevents reverse loading of the top bearings. End play is limited by shims when the thrust block is shrunk on the shaft or by tightening the locknut on the shaft above the bearing mounting sleeve. The thrust bearings on 2 pole motors are mounted directly on the shaft and do not require an adjustment by the shims or locknut.

[4] Nidec Motor Manual, p. 24 · I. Spherical Roller Thrust Bearings and Angular Contact Bearings (With Springs)
On spherical roller or angular contact thrust bearings with springs, setting the correct end play for preload requires a controlled assembly method, due to various deflections internal to the motor and friction of locknut threads from spring force. An end play setting of .005 to .008 inches is required to allow the lower guide bearing to return to an unload position when external thrust is applied to the motor (see Figure 5). End play can be properly adjusted by the following recommended procedure:
- A. Place spring retainer, without springs and lower thrust washer of bearing, into upper bracket bearing bore.
- B. Using a depth micrometer, measure the distance between the top of the lower thrust washer and the faced surface on top of the bearing housing. Record this dimension to three decimal places.
- C. Add .005 and .008 inches to the recorded dimension to obtain the correct minimum and maximum settings range for the unit.
- D. Reassemble bearing with springs; motor is now ready to set end play.
NOTE: Certain motor builds require removal of the fabricated steel or cast aluminum oil baffle to provide access for depth micrometer measurements.
Motors built with spherical roller thrust or angular contact bearings with springs require a minimum external thrust load, sufficient to compress upper die springs and unload lower guide bearing from axial spring thrust. Refer to the motor's spring thrust plate for required minimum thrust.
NOTE: Do not run motor without load for more than fifteen minutes, as lower bearing damage may occur and improper seating of thrust bearing may cause vibration.

[5] Siemens Manual Vertical Induction Motors EN, p. 35 · Vertical Solid & Hollow Shaft Nomenclature
Angular Contact Bearing - An antifriction thrust bearing capable of taking high thrust in one axial direction only.
DT Bearing - Two (2) angular contact bearings mounted together to take extra high thrust in one axial direction only.
DB Bearings - Two (2) angular contact bearings mounted together such that each one will take high thrust in opposite directions.
End Play - The axial movement of the shaft.
Four Point Bearing - An angular contact bearing which will take thrust in both directions.
Guide Bearing - The bearing mounted in the housing opposite the thrust bearing. Most are deep groove antifriction bearings.
Thrust block or Bearing Mounting Sleeve - The member keyed to the motor shaft on which the inner race of the thrust bearing is mounted.
Continuous Down Thrust - The thrust developed by the weight of the pump shaft and hydraulic unbalance. This is the thrust value to which the motor thrust bearings are sized.
Maximum Down Thrust - the momentary down thrust that can be developed during shut down of the pump.
Momentary Upthrust - This thrust may develop in some shallow settings during startup. Momentary upthrust is mostly carried by the Guide Bearing in most vertical motors.
Non-Reverse Ratchet or Backstop - A device that permits motor to turn in only one direction. It is used mostly in conjunction with Rigid Couplings to prevent turbine pump backspin caused by the water column receding when the motor is de-energized.

results.question: For a hollow shaft Siemens motor, what dial indicator reading is the limit for acceptable alignment?
results.expected_answer: Readings must not exceed 0.0005 inches at 90-degree increments
results.rewritten_query: Siemens hollow-shaft motor: What is the maximum permissible dial indicator reading for acceptable alignment?
results.answer:
For a **hollow-shaft Siemens motor**, acceptable alignment is when the dial indicator readings **do not exceed 0.0005 inches**. [2]

Procedure:

1. Clamp the dial indicator to the pump shaft, align it with the basebolt plane, and set it to zero. [2]
2. Remove the top cover and rotate both the unit and pump shafts. [2]
3. Read the indicator at 90-degree increments from the starting point. [2]
4. Accept the alignment only when the readings do not exceed **0.0005 inches**. [2]
5. Shim the flange faces if necessary. [2]

The shaft runout is measured with the indicator stationary with respect to the machine and with its point at the end of the finished surface of the shaft. See Figure 13 for typical fixture.

Hollow shaft units require accurate alignment with respect to the unit shaft and the driven/drive equipment shaft. The pump shaft acts as a pendulum supported by the top coupling and unit bearing.

The following checking procedure applies to a unit consisting of motor/generator, coupling, and a driven/drive component. Although applicable to most types of couplings, it is primarily intended for the rabbet-fit type. Work in one plane at a time and test for parallel or angular alignment with a dial indicator mounted as shown in Figure 1. Proceed as follows:

This method uses a one inch thick steel disc, with center hole for shaft end bolt, and two threaded hydraulic jacks connected to a single pump. results.question: What drying temperature does Siemens give for Class F insulation, and what must be done before reaching it?
results.expected_answer: 245°F (118°C); Class F and H units are first baked at 70% of the specified temperature for about six hours
results.rewritten_query: Siemens recommended drying temperature for Class F motor insulation and required actions before reaching that temperature.
results.answer:
## Direct answer

Siemens specifies the following drying temperature for **Class F insulation**:

| Insulation class | Drying temperature |
|---|---:|
| Class F | **245°F (118°C)** [1] |

Before raising the temperature to 245°F (118°C), bake Class F insulation at **70% of the specified temperature for about six hours** to avoid steam forming inside the winding. [1]

## Procedure and conditions

1. Confirm that inadequate insulation resistance is believed to result from excessive moisture in the windings. [1]
2. Apply heat using a warm-air oven, electric strip heaters, or circulating currents through the coils. [1]
3. Apply the heat slowly; the desired temperature should not be reached in less than six hours. [1]
4. For Class F insulation, hold the windings at 70% of the specified drying temperature for about six hours before increasing to 245°F (118°C). [1]
5. Measure insulation resistance before applying heat and every six to eight hours thereafter. [1]

If electric strip heaters are used:

1. Remove the bearing housings. [3]
2. Remove the rotor. [3]
3. Direct a fan at the stator to carry away moisture. [3]
4. Attach temperature indicators to the winding and apply heat according to the drying-temperature table and the stated drying procedure. [3]
5. Do not use radiant-type heaters, because some parts may scorch before remote parts reach the desired temperature. [3]

Question: After requesting a motor equipped with class "F" insulation, I received a unit on which the insulation class is labeled "B." Was there a mix-up in my order?

These limits are 80 degrees centigrade at 1.0 service factor, and 90 degrees centigrade at 1.15 service factor. For many years, it has been our policy to nameplate open dripproof motors that meet this temperature rise criteria with the insulation class "B", regardless of the actual insulation type. This gives the end user the information that the motor has a 90 degrees centigrade, or less, temperature rise at 1.15 service factor.

contexts:
[1] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · 7.5.3.3 Re-greasing intervals
Rolling bearings of electrical machines need to be re-greased at regular intervals. The re-greasing interval is found on the bearing plate.
NOTE:
Regardless of the re-greasing interval, the bearings need to be re-greased at least once per year.
The re-greasing intervals are calculated for an operating temperature of 70°C (160°F). If the operating temperature is lower or higher than the assumed, the re-grease interval has to be altered accordingly. Higher operating temperature decreases the re-greasing interval.
NOTE:
An increase in the ambient temperature raises the temperature of the bearings correspondingly. The values for the re-greasing interval should be halved for every 15°C (30°F) increase in bearing temperature and may be once doubled for a 15°C (30°F) decrease in bearing temperature.

[2] Nidec Motor Manual, p. 29 · Lubrication Instructions
Question: How can motors in service be relubricated?
Answer Units are pre-lubricated at the factory and do not require initial lubrication. Relubricating interval depends upon speed, type of bearing and service. Refer to table in the Operating and Instruction Manual provided with motor for suggested re-greasing intervals and recommended greases. Operating conditions may dictate more frequent lubrication. Motor must be at rest and electrical controls should be locked open to prevent energizing while motor is being serviced (refer to section on Safety). If motor is being taken out of storage, refer to storage procedures.
To re-lubricate bearings, remove the drain plug. Inspect grease drain and remove any blockage with a mechanical probe taking care not to damage bearing. Under no circumstances should a mechanical probe be used while the motor is in operation. Add new grease at the grease inlet. New grease must be compatible with grease already in the motor (refer to Table 1 in Operating & Maintenance Manual for replenishment quantities). Run the motor for 15 to 30 minutes with the drain plug removed to allow purging of any excess grease. Shut off unit and replace the drain plug. Return motor to service.

[3] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 84 · 7.5.2.5 Oil change schedule for mineral oils
For self-lubricated bearings cleaning intervals with oil changes of approximately 8000 operating hours are recommended and approx. 20000 operating hours for bearings with oil circulation systems.
Shorter oil change intervals may be necessary in case of frequent start-ups, high oil temperatures or excessively high contamination due to external influences.
The correct oil change interval can be found on the bearing plate and dimensional drawing, see Chapter 2.1.2 Bearing plate.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 66 · Figure 32 Example of lubrication channel through bearing arrangement of horizontal machine
NOTE:
NOTE:
Start-up greasing may take several grease portions (3-10 times amount mentioned at the lubrication plate).
The re-lubrication interval will never be longer than 12 months.
The type of original grease used is found on the bearing plate on the machine. Acceptable types of grease can be found in Chapter 7.5.3 Rolling bearings.
NOTE:
Do not mix greases! There must be only one type of grease inside the bearing - not mixture of two or more greases.
The temperature of the bearings will initially increase because of the excess grease. After few hours, the excess grease will be discharged through the lubrication valve and the temperature of the bearing will return to normal running temperature.
If available, and after the machine has been running for several hours, measure the vibrations or SPM-values from the SPM-nipples, and record the values for future reference use.
Following chapter for bearing type: Sleeve bearing

[5] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 85 · 7.5.3.4 Re-greasing
All rolling bearings of rotating electrical machines need to be re-greased, see Chapter 7.5.3.3 Re-greasing intervals. The re-greasing can be performed either manually or by means of an automatic system. In either case, it has to be verified that a suitable amount of the correct grease is entering the bearing at suitable intervals.
NOTE:
Grease can cause skin irritation and eye inflammation. Follow all safety precautions specified by the grease manufacturer.

- The value applies to screws with **standard threads**; fine-thread screws require a specific tightening instruction. [1]

- Do not apply it to a **metric screw fitting**, since the Kohler manual provides separate torque values for series L and series S fittings. [3][5]
- The provided context does not contain a separate KD27V12-specific override, tightening sequence, lubrication condition, or torque tolerance; these would need to be verified in the applicable engine instruction if relevant.

results.question: If the fuel sulfur content is between 0.5% and 1%, how does the Kohler engine oil change interval change?
results.expected_answer: Oil change factor 1/2 — the interval is halved; limited to engine oil categories 2 and 3
results.rewritten_query: Kohler engine oil change interval for fuel sulfur content between 0.5% and 1%.
results.answer:
## Change interval

For fuel sulfur content **greater than 0.5% and up to 1%**, the oil-change factor is **1/2**, so the engine oil change interval is **reduced by half**. This range is limited to **engine oil categories 2 and 3**. [1]

| Fuel sulfur content | Oil-change factor | Effect on interval | Condition |
|---|---:|---|---|
| \(0.5\% < \text{sulfur} \leq 1\%\) | \(1/2\) | Interval reduced by half | Limited to engine oil categories 2 and 3 [1] |

The calculation is:

$$
\text{Change interval}
=
\text{Basic interval}
\times
\text{Oil-category factor}
\times
\frac{1}{2}
$$

The context does not provide the applicable basic interval or oil-category factor, so an absolute interval in operating hours cannot be calculated from the supplied information.

## Maintenance procedure

1. Confirm that the measured fuel sulfur content is above \(0.5\%\) and no greater than \(1\%\). [1]
2. Apply a sulfur-content factor of \(1/2\), subject to using engine oil category 2 or 3. [1]
3. If difficult operating conditions apply—such as frequent cold starts, dust, high humidity, long downtimes, environmental influences, or operating-temperature effects—validate the interval through engine oil analysis. [1]
4. Use engine oil analysis to monitor the oil and adjust the change interval if required. [5]

results.answer:
## Conservation protection duration

In normal storage in a **dry, ventilated place**, the engine’s conservation protection lasts **6 months from the date it is ready for delivery**. [1]

For longer storage, the stated protection period should **not be assumed to remain valid**: the manual says that more unfavorable conditions—such as longer outdoor storage or damp, unventilated storage—are expected to shorten the conservation protection period. [1]

- With an additional film cover, the conserved engine may be stored **outdoors for up to 1 month**. [1]
- The cover must be **waterproof**, lie **loosely** against the engine, allow air circulation, and prevent condensation formation. [1]
- Storage conditions are the responsibility of the system manufacturer, and only preservatives approved by Kohler may be used. [2]

The provided context does not specify a revised conservation period or a detailed preservation procedure for storage beyond six months.

## Charge generator belt tension

The provided context does **not specify the correct belt-tension value or limit**, nor does it state **when the tension must be reset**. Therefore, the required tension and reset interval/condition cannot be determined from the available excerpts.

results.rewritten_query: EMSA generator engine manuals: recommended engine oil, antifreeze/coolant type, and antifreeze-to-water mixing ratio.
results.answer:
## Recommendation

- **Engine oil:** The context does not specify an oil brand, viscosity grade, or formulation. It instructs the user to use the recommended lubricant and to verify suitability against the viscosity–temperature diagram for the regional temperature conditions. [3][4]
- **Antifreeze:** Use antifreeze mixed with water in the radiator; the stated average ratio is **50% antifreeze**, adjusted as required by regional conditions. [4]
- **Factory condition:** Antifreeze is **not supplied in the radiator from the factory**. [4]

## Procedure

1. Select the engine oil using the manual’s viscosity–temperature diagram for the operating temperatures in the region. [4]
2. Add antifreeze to the radiator with water at the ratio required by regional conditions; use **50% antifreeze as the average reference ratio**. [4]
3. Maintain the water-and-antifreeze mixture throughout the year to support the service life of the engine and coolant pipes. [4]
4. If the exact oil specification or regional antifreeze ratio is required, consult the complete viscosity chart or an EMSA authorized service, because those details are not included in the provided context. [3][4]

results.question: When adding electrolyte to an EMSA maintenance-type battery for the first time, what density and level are required, and how long is the minimum charge?
results.expected_answer: Specific density 1.280 at 20°C, filled to 15 mm above the plates (electrolyte above 10°C); minimum charging period 6 hours
results.rewritten_query: EMSA maintenance-type battery: during initial electrolyte filling, what electrolyte density and level are required, and what is the minimum charging time?
results.answer:
## Required values

- **Electrolyte density:** $1.270$–$1.280$ specific density, corresponding to a fully charged battery. The context does not state a separate density specifically for the initial filling. [2]
- **Electrolyte level:** Add distilled water until the electrolyte is **10 mm above the plates**. [1]
- **Minimum charge/confirmation period:** Check the electrolyte level every hour; the battery is considered charged when **no change is observed after one hour**. [1]

## Procedure

1. Add electrolyte to the maintenance-type battery. The context does not provide a separate initial-fill quantity or density beyond the fully charged range above. [1][2]
2. Charge the battery while checking the electrolyte level at **1-hour intervals**. [1]
3. Confirm charging when the electrolyte level shows **no change for one hour**. [1]
4. Add distilled water as necessary to maintain the level **10 mm above the plates**. [1]

This maintenance instruction must be fully implemented periodically to maintain radiator efficiency and warranty support coverage. If any maintenance steps are missed, any warranty issues may not be covered by EMSA.
- The radiator must be filled slowly and carefully, leaving no air space inside.
- Balance and order must be ensured by checking the physical condition of the fan blades.
- The tension of the belts connecting the engine and radiator ulleys must also be checked for looseness, cracks, damage or defects. After the checks, loose belts must be tightened and damaged belts should be replaced.
High voltage values on belts/pulleys will shorten their life. Low tension values will cause deformation in the bands, causing the speed to decrease (cooling performance to decrease) or the radiator to be damaged.
- In order not to make any adjustments at the bottom of the radiator and to ensure that the coolant remains homogeneous, he engine must be started at predetermined intervals (by the engine manufacturer) and the radiator's coolant must be circulated periodically.
- No foreign substance or any substance other than the coolant mixture (antifreeze, water, some protective chemicals…) must be placed or dripped into the radiator.
- Radiators that have not been used for 6 months or more must be washed and cleaned inside before use.
- Necessary measures must be taken against vibration, especially between the radiator and chassis connection.
- Lifting lugs must be used as handles when lifting the radiator.
- The radiator cap must be replaced once a year.
- While carrying the radiator, the user should be very careful to avoid damage to the radiator's connection points (welding, bolts, etc.).
- Radiators must be protected from humidity and similar conditions.

[2] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 57 · 4.3.5 Insulation distances of main power connections
The connections of the main power cables must be designed to withstand demanding operation conditions where the insulators can be subjected to dirt, humidity and surge voltages. In order to ensure lasting and trouble-free running, it is therefore important that the length of the insulation and creepage distances are sufficient. The minimum insulation and creepage distances should be equal or exceed demands set by:
- Local requirements
- Standards
- Classification rules
- Hazardous area classification.
The insulation and creepage distances apply both for insulation distances between two different phases, and for insulation distances between one phase and earth. The air insulation distance is the shortest distance through air between two points with different electrical potential (voltage). The surface creepage distance is the shortest distance along surfaces next to each other between two points with different electrical potential (voltage).

The auxiliary cables must be screened to meet the EMC requirements. Special cable glands must be used for the 360° high-frequency earthing of the cable screens at the cable entries.

[4] ABB Manual for Induction Motors and Generators EN, p. 59 · 4.3.10.2 Earthing of main cable
The compliance with EMC directive requires high-frequency earthing of the main cable. This is achieved by a 360° earthing of the cable screens at the cable entries in both the machine and in the frequency converter. The earthing at the machine is implemented for example by means of the EMC ROX SYSTEM cable transits for shielded installations.
NOTE:
360° high-frequency earthing of cable entries is made in order to suppress electromagnetic disturbances. In addition, cable screens have to be connected to protective earth (PE) in order to meet safety regulations.

results.question: What service life is declared for EMSA generators?
results.expected_answer: 10 years, per the after-sales services regulation (Official Gazette No. 29029, 13 June 2014)
results.rewritten_query: What service life is specified for EMSA generators in the maintenance manuals?
results.answer:
## Declared service life

The provided EMSA documentation does **not declare a total service life** for the generators. It declares a **2-year warranty period**, but this is not stated as the generator’s service life. [3]

The EMSA manual only specifies that:

- Periodic inspections and maintenance must be performed completely and on time; faults caused by missing periodic maintenance are excluded from warranty coverage. [2]
- Maintenance, adjustment, and repair must be performed by authorized services or qualified personnel using genuine parts. [1]
- The generator is intended to provide long service life when operated and maintained according to the manual. [2]

The **8-year** intervals shown in the context belong to the Kohler generator maintenance schedules, not to an EMSA-declared service-life specification. [4][5]

Therefore, the service-life value for EMSA generators is **not specified in the provided context**.

It is essential to use grease of good quality and with the correct base soap. This will ensure a long and trouble free lifetime of the bearings.
Grease used for re-greasing should have the following properties:
- Be special rolling bearing grease.
- Be of good quality with a lithium complex soap, and with mineral-, or PAO-oil.
- Have a base oil viscosity of 100 to 160 cSt at 40°C (105°F).
- Have a consistency NLGI grade between 1.5 and 3. For vertically or in hot conditions mounted machines, NLGI grade 2 or 3 is recommended.
- Have a continuous temperature range between -30°C (-20°F) and at least +120°C (250°F).
Grease with the correct properties is available from all major lubricant manufacturers. If the make of grease is changed and compatibility is uncertain, consult the manufacturing ABB factory, see Chapter 9.1.3 Contact information for Motors and Generators Service.

- The original viscosity must be maintained within a tolerance of ±15%.
- The oil should be free from debris, and its cleanliness according to ISO 4406 class 18/15, or NAS 1638 class 9.
- The quantity of metal impurities should be less than 100 PPM. An increasing trend of the value means that the bearing is wearing.
- The total acid number (TAN) should not exceed 1 mg KOH per gram of oil. Please note that the TAN value is not the same as the TBN (total base number) value.
- Smell the oil. Strong acid or burnt smell is not acceptable.
An oil check should be performed a few days after the first test run of the machine, just before the first oil change, and subsequently as required. If the oil is changed just after the commissioning, it can be used again after removing wear particles by filtering or centrifuging.
In doubtful cases, an oil sample may be sent to the laboratory to determine viscosity, acid number, foaming tendency, etc.
